originalTitle: Borges and Me review – a sweetly imagined literary odyssey through the Highlands
summary: Luis Gnecco brings warmth, wit and quiet melancholy to Jorge Luis Borges in this gently enchanting adaptation of Jay Parini’s semi-fictional memoir
content: There is great sweetness and high-minded, unworldly charm in this adaptation of American author Jay Parini’s embellished memoir, a romantic account of his road trip through the Scottish Highlands that, as a young doctoral student at St Andrews in 1971, he really did take with Jorge Luis Borges, the great writer whose blindness had become part of his mystique. Author of poetry, enigmatic short stories and metaphysical vignettes untranslatably known as the “ficciones”, Borges is described here as “the father of magical realism” – although he is surely more unique and interesting than that. Parini drives Borges around, describes everything to the maestro (who is rapt and beaming), and shields him when he uninhibitedly urinates in public; all the while he is almost entirely unaware of Borges’ reputation and the enormous honour that this therefore was. Fionn Whitehead plays the callow young Parini, in specs and duffle coat resembling a young Tom Courtenay, wretched that he may have inadvertently persuaded his brother Billy back home to volunteer for military service in Vietnam. He is ungratefully grumpy that he has to spend time away from his PhD for this babysitting task, assigned to him by his supervisor, poet and Borges translator Alastair Reid, played by Alan Cumming. Borges himself is entertainingly played by the Chilean actor Luis Gnecco; priestly, childlike, mischievous and sly, a performance executed with theatrical panache – I can imagine him doing it on stage – but without hammily overdoing the milky-eyed upward gaze. His Borges is a man who like all charming people has cultivated a dependency on others, and we can see how he has had a lifetime to deploy the combination of his huge reputation and the poignant helplessness of the blind. He has come to Scotland without a nurse or amanuensis and has to rely on the (cowed) kindness of strangers. Parini and Borges are like Sancho Panza and Don Quixote, whose presence is duly hallucinated at one stage, though it is odd that Borges, that profound Scotophile, does not specifically invoke Boswell and Johnson in the Outer Hebrides. It may be that screenwriter Oren Moverman, or Parini himself, is influenced by Gore Vidal’s memories of guiding around his blind grandfather, US senator Thomas Pryor Gore, whom he described as a “passionate sightseer”. Borges himself, in this film, on being introduced to the hesitant Parini, whimsically says: “Speak up – I am blind!” Borges is a huge Bob Dylan fan – and, apropos Vietnam, anti-war – although the script does not specifically anticipate Borges’ description of the Falklands war: two bald men fighting over a comb. The source material is avowedly fictionalised and unreliable, and this is never more obvious here than in the fanciful scene in which Borges demands to be rowed by Parini out into the middle of Loch Ness so he can commune with the monster’s presence – and actually falls in the water, supposedly gets rescued by Parini and the film cuts sharply to Borges cordially drying off later in the local pub. Try clambering into a rowboat from the water and you’ll know how plausible this is. But maybe Parini and Borges swam to shore. And yet in many ways, the story does have the ring of truth – particularly in the section in which Parini has to talk to a second and entirely different twinkle-eyed literary legend, the poet George Mackay Brown, on whom Parini is supposed to be writing his PhD, played with opaque geniality by Peter Mullan. If this story was simply fictional, introducing a second figure of this sort would be struck out by any script editor as being an unnecessary duplication. But this is the messy wrongness of real life. The title alludes to Borges’ story Borges and I, which reflects on the difference between the writer’s public persona and his private identity. For almost the entire film, the indefatigable Borges seems to be putting on an act and yet, while quizzing Parini on his amorous adventures with a local woman (Freya Mavor), he reveals something of his own loneliness and regret. The effect is genuinely affecting and sad, and it is a lovely performance from Gnecco. • Borges and Me screened at the Edinburgh film festival.
chineseTitle: 《博尔赫斯与我》评论——一场穿越高地的甜蜜想象的文学冒险之旅
chineseSummary: 路易斯·尼科在这部改编自杰·帕里尼半虚构回忆录的温柔迷人的作品中，为豪尔赫·路易斯·博尔赫斯带来了温暖、机智和安静的忧郁
chineseContent: 这部改编自美国作家杰伊·帕里尼 (Jay Parini) 精心修饰的回忆录的作品充满了甜蜜和高尚、超凡脱俗的魅力，浪漫地描述了他穿越苏格兰高地的公路旅行，1971 年，作为圣安德鲁斯的一名年轻博士生，他确实与豪尔赫·路易斯·博尔赫斯 (Jorge Luis Borges) 在一起，这位伟大的作家的失明已成为他神秘感的一部分。博尔赫斯是诗歌、神秘短篇小说和形而上学短篇小说的作者，无法翻译地被称为“小说”，他在这里被描述为“魔幻现实主义之父”——尽管他肯定比这更独特和有趣。帕里尼开车带着博尔赫斯四处走动，向这位大师（全神贯注、笑容可掬）描述一切，并在他在公共场合不加抑制地小便时保护他；一直以来，他几乎完全不知道博尔赫斯的声誉以及由此带来的巨大荣誉。菲恩·怀特海德 (Fionn Whitehead) 饰演稚气未脱的年轻帕里尼 (Parini)，戴着眼镜，穿着粗呢大衣，酷似年轻的汤姆·康特尼 (Tom Courtenay)，他很不幸，因为他可能无意中说服了他的兄弟比利 (Billy) 回国志愿去越南服兵役。他忘恩负义地脾气暴躁，因为他不得不花时间远离他的博士学位来完成这项保姆任务，这项任务是由他的导师、诗人和博尔赫斯翻译家阿拉斯泰尔·里德（艾伦·卡明饰演）分配给他的。博尔赫斯本人由智利演员路易斯·格内科 (Luis Gnecco) 有趣地饰演。牧师般的、孩子气的、顽皮的、狡猾的，表演充满了戏剧性的气派——我可以想象他在舞台上的表现——但又没有过度夸张地向上凝视着乳白色的眼睛。他的博尔赫斯像所有迷人的人一样培养了对他人的依赖，我们可以看到他如何用一生来部署他巨大的声誉和盲人的辛酸无助的结合。他来到苏格兰时带着
